---
title: Creating projects with `q2 create`
---

## Overview

`q2 create` scaffolds a new Quarto project: it creates a directory
containing a `_quarto.yml` configuration file and starter documents
that `q2 render` can build immediately.

```bash
q2 create project website mysite
```

```default
Created project in mysite:

  created  _quarto.yml
  created  index.qmd
  created  about.qmd
  created  styles.css
  created  .gitignore

To render it: q2 render mysite
```

## Interactive use

Run `q2 create` with no arguments on a terminal and it walks you
through the choices: the artifact type, the project type, the
directory, and the title (pre-filled with a sensible default you can
accept or edit).

Prompting only happens on a real interactive terminal. When stdin or
stderr is redirected, when running under CI, or when you pass
`--no-prompt`, missing arguments are errors instead — so scripts never
hang waiting for input.

## Command-line use

The non-interactive form spells everything out:

```bash
q2 create project <type> <directory> [title]
```

- `<type>` is a project type: `default` (a minimal project) or
  `website` (a website with navigation). The types `blog`,
  `manuscript`, and `book` are recognized but not yet implemented in
  Quarto 2.
- `<directory>` is where the project is created, relative to the
  current directory. Use `.` to scaffold into the current directory.
- `[title]` is the project title. When omitted, the title defaults to
  the directory name (or to the project type name when the directory
  is `.`), and a warning tells you which default was used:

  ```default
  Warning: No title provided; using "mysite" as the project title
  ```

To see the available artifact and project types, run `q2 create --list`:

```default
Available artifact types:

project (Project)
  default      A minimal Quarto project
  website      A Quarto website with navigation
  blog         A blog using the Quarto blog template (not yet implemented)
  manuscript   An academic manuscript (not yet implemented)
  book         A multi-chapter book (not yet implemented)

Usage: q2 create project <type> <directory> [title]
```

## What gets created

A `website` project contains a configuration file, two pages wired
into a navbar, and an empty stylesheet:

``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
project:
  type: website
  resources:
    - styles.css

website:
  title: "mysite"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - about.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
    toc: true
```

A `default` project is a minimal `_quarto.yml` (just the project
title) plus a starter `index.qmd`.

Both project types also write a `.gitignore` containing `/.quarto/`,
the directory Quarto uses for caches and other machinery it writes
into the project tree.

## Directory semantics

- The target directory is created if it doesn't exist. Creating into
  an **existing** directory is allowed.
- If the directory already contains a `_quarto.yml` or `_quarto.yaml`,
  the command fails before writing anything:

  ```default
  Error: Directory 'mysite' already contains a Quarto project
  Found _quarto.yml. Choose a different directory.
  ```

- Files that already exist are skipped individually, so scaffolding
  into a non-empty directory never overwrites your files:

  ```default
    created  _quarto.yml
    created  index.qmd
    created  about.qmd
    skipped-existing styles.css (already exists, skipped)
    created  .gitignore
  ```

- If a `.gitignore` already exists, the `/.quarto/` entry is appended
  only when missing; the rest of the file is left untouched.

## Dry runs

Pass `--dry-run` to see the full file plan — including per-file
created/skipped decisions and the already-a-project check — without
writing anything:

```bash
q2 create project website mysite "My Site" --dry-run
```

```default
(dry run) would create project in mysite:

  created  _quarto.yml
  created  index.qmd
  created  about.qmd
  created  styles.css
  created  .gitignore

(dry run) nothing was written.
```

## Machine interface {#machine-interface}

Tools that drive project creation programmatically — editors, language
servers, MCP servers — can use the JSON interface instead of
positional arguments. It follows one convention throughout:
**stdout carries exactly one JSON result; all diagnostics (errors and
warnings) go to stderr as JSON lines.** The command never prompts in
this mode.

### Creating a project

`q2 create --json` reads a single JSON *directive* from stdin and
writes a JSON *result* to stdout:

```bash
echo '{"artifact": "project", "directory": "mysite",
       "choice": "website", "title": "My Site"}' | q2 create --json
```

The directive fields for the `project` artifact:

| Field       | Required | Meaning                                              |
|-------------|----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| `artifact`  | yes      | Artifact type; currently `"project"`                 |
| `directory` | yes      | Target directory, relative to the working directory  |
| `choice`    | yes      | Project type (`"default"`, `"website"`, …)           |
| `title`     | no       | Project title; same defaulting as the CLI path       |
| `dry_run`   | no       | Compute the file plan but write nothing              |

Unknown fields are rejected, so misspelled keys fail loudly instead of
being silently ignored.

On success the command exits 0 and prints the result:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "path": "/absolute/path/to/mysite",
  "dry_run": false,
  "files": [
    { "path": "_quarto.yml", "action": "created" },
    { "path": "index.qmd", "action": "created" },
    { "path": "about.qmd", "action": "created" },
    { "path": "styles.css", "action": "created" },
    { "path": ".gitignore", "action": "created" }
  ]
}
```

`version` identifies the result shape (currently `1`). `path` is the
absolute path of the project directory. Each file reports an
`action`: `"created"`, or `"skipped-existing"` when the file was
already present. With `"dry_run": true` (or the `--dry-run` flag,
which is equivalent), the same result is reported with
`"dry_run": true` and nothing is written.

### Errors and warnings

On failure the command exits non-zero, writes **nothing** to stdout,
and emits a structured error on stderr as a JSON line:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://quarto.org/schemas/v1/json-diagnostic.json",
  "kind": "error",
  "title": "Unknown project type 'nope'",
  "problem": "Valid project types: default, website. Not yet implemented: blog, manuscript, book.",
  "hints": [],
  "details": []
}
```

Warnings use the same shape with `"kind": "warning"` — for example the
defaulted-title warning when the directive omits `title`. Since
diagnostics never mix into stdout, callers can always parse stdout as
a single JSON document.

### Discovering capabilities

`q2 create --list --json` emits the registry of artifact types and
their choices, so tools can populate pickers without hardcoding the
type list:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "artifacts": [
    {
      "type": "project",
      "display_name": "Project",
      "choices": [
        {
          "id": "default",
          "name": "Default",
          "description": "A minimal Quarto project",
          "implemented": true
        },
        {
          "id": "website",
          "name": "Website",
          "description": "A Quarto website with navigation",
          "implemented": true
        },
        {
          "id": "blog",
          "name": "Blog",
          "description": "A blog using the Quarto blog template",
          "implemented": false
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

(The full listing also includes `manuscript` and `book`.) Offer only
choices with `"implemented": true`; the others are reserved and
rejected if used in a directive.
